Savour no more thanne the byhove schal; Reule weel thiself, that other folk canst reede; And trouthe schal delyvere, it is no drede. Myche wele stant in litel besynesse; Bywar therfore to spurne ayeyns an al; Stryve not as doth the crokke with the wal. Daunte thiself, that dauntest otheres dede; And trouthe shal delyvere, it is no drede. That the is sent, receyve in buxumnesse; The wrestlyng for the worlde axeth a fal. Here is non home, here nys but wyldernesse. Forth, pylgryme, forth! forth, beste, out of thi stal! Know thi contré! loke up! thonk God of al! Hold the heye weye, and lat thi gost the lede; And trouthe shal delyvere, it is no drede. Therfore, thou Vache, leve thine olde wrechednesse; Unto the world leve now to be thral. prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Flee from worldly crowds and live with truth, being content with your own possessions even if they are small.
- Avoid greed, ambition, envy, and excessive desire, because worldly wealth and status are unstable and deceptive.
- Govern yourself humbly instead of trying to correct everything or struggle against forces beyond your control.
- Accept what is given to you obediently, remember that life is a pilgrimage rather than a permanent home, and let your spirit guide you toward God.
- Leave behind servitude to the world, seek God’s mercy, and pray for heavenly reward for yourself and others.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Fle, Suffise, For

outputs.L1:
Flee from the crowd, and dwell with truthfulness.  
Be content with what is your own, though it be small;  
for hoarding breeds hatred, and climbing brings uncertainty.  
The crowd has envy, and prosperity blinds all around.  
Desire no more than necessity requires.  
Govern yourself well, you who know how to counsel others;  
and truth shall deliver you—there is no doubt.

Do not trouble yourself to set every crooked thing straight,  
trusting in Fortune, who turns like a ball.  
Great well-being often lies in little busyness;  
therefore beware of kicking against an awl.  
Do not strive like the earthen pot against the wall.  
Master yourself, you who would master the deeds of others;  
and truth shall deliver you—there is no doubt.

Receive with humility whatever is sent to you;  
wrestling for the world calls for a fall.  
Here is no true home; here is only wilderness.  
Onward, pilgrim, onward! Onward, beast, out of your stall!  
Know your true country; look upward; thank God for all.  
Keep to the high road, and let your spirit lead you;  
and truth shall deliver you—there is no doubt.

Therefore, you Vache, leave behind your old wretchedness;  
cease now to be a slave to the world.  
Cry for mercy to Him who, in His high goodness,  
made you from nothing, and in particular  
draw near to Him, and pray in general  
for yourself and also for others, for heavenly reward;  
and truth shall deliver you—there is no doubt.
outputs.L2:
Run from the crowd and live in honesty.  
Be content with what is yours, even if it is little.  
Hoarded wealth brings hatred, and ambition is unstable;  
Public life attracts envy, and prosperity blinds people everywhere.  
Desire only what you truly need.  
Govern yourself well, since you know how to advise others.  
Truth will set you free—there is no doubt of it.

Do not exhaust yourself trying to straighten every crooked thing,  
Especially not by trusting Fortune, who spins like a ball.  
Great happiness can exist in a quiet, simple life.  
So be careful not to kick against a spike.  
Do not struggle like a clay pot fighting a wall.  
Master yourself, you who judge the actions of others.  
Truth will set you free—there is no doubt of it.

Accept obediently whatever is given to you.  
To wrestle for worldly gain is to invite a fall.  
This world is not your true home; it is only a wilderness.  
Go forward, pilgrim—go on! Leave your stall like a beast set loose.  
Remember your true homeland; look upward, and thank God for everything.  
Stay on the high road, and let your spirit guide you.  
Truth will set you free—there is no doubt of it.

Therefore, you, Vache, abandon your old misery.  
Stop being a slave to the world.  
Beg mercy from the One who, out of His great goodness,  
Created you from nothing and especially draws you toward Him.  
Pray to Him, both for yourself and for others,  
That you may receive heavenly reward.  
Truth will set you free—there is no doubt of it.
outputs.L3:
Flee from the noise and confusion of worldly crowds, and choose instead to live in the company of truth. Do not measure your life by the wealth, praise, or approval of others. Be content with what you possess, even if it seems small, for peace is not found in abundance but in a quiet and faithful heart. A person who is satisfied with little is richer than one who has much but is always restless for more.

Guard yourself against greed, ambition, envy, and excessive desire. These passions promise happiness, but they often lead only to anxiety and disappointment. Worldly wealth can disappear, honor can be taken away, and status can change in a moment. What seems secure is often unstable, and what appears glorious may be deceptive. Therefore, do not place your hope in possessions or reputation, but seek the things that endure.

Learn to govern yourself with humility. It is better to rule your own thoughts, desires, and actions than to attempt to correct everything around you. Do not exhaust yourself struggling against circumstances beyond your control or trying to force the world to conform to your will. Accept your limits, act with patience, and cultivate inner discipline. In humility, you will find a strength greater than pride can offer.

Receive obediently what is given to you, whether it is ease or hardship, abundance or want. Remember that this life is a pilgrimage, not a permanent dwelling place. You are a traveler passing through, and your true home is not found in the passing things of the world. Let your spirit, purified by faith and guided by grace, lead you toward God. Walk with attentiveness, knowing that every step can bring you closer to Him.

Leave behind servitude to the world and its empty promises. Seek the mercy of God above all else, for His compassion is greater than human weakness and His reward surpasses every earthly gain. Pray not only for yourself, but also for others, that all may be freed from vain desires, strengthened in goodness, and brought at last to the joy of heaven.
outputs.L4:
The poem reflects on the dangers of becoming too attached to worldly ambition, status, wealth, and praise. It warns that the desire to rise above others can easily lead to envy, pride, restlessness, and moral confusion. When people measure their worth by comparison, they become trapped by dissatisfaction: they resent the success of others, fear failure, and lose sight of what is truly valuable. In this way, the poem presents worldly striving not as a path to happiness, but as a source of anxiety and spiritual danger.

Against these temptations, the poem urges a humbler and wiser way of living. Rather than trying to control others or chase every desire, a person should first learn self-governance: mastery over one’s own thoughts, emotions, and actions. Contentment is shown as a form of strength, not weakness, because it frees the soul from constant craving. Patience also becomes essential, since human life is uncertain and often difficult. The poem suggests that peace comes not from forcing life to match personal ambition, but from accepting one’s limits and trusting in a higher divine order.

The image of life as a pilgrimage gives the poem a spiritual direction. Human beings are not meant to treat the world as a permanent possession, but as a journey through which the soul is tested, refined, and guided. Suffering, delay, and disappointment can become part of this journey if they lead a person away from pride and toward deeper faith. By turning toward God and relying on divine truth rather than worldly illusion, the individual finds deliverance from fear, envy, and attachment.

Ultimately, the poem teaches that truth is the path to spiritual freedom and peace. Worldly ambition promises fulfillment but often creates bondage; divine truth, by contrast, liberates the soul. To live truthfully is to live with humility, patience, self-control, and trust. The poem concludes that those who accept life as a pilgrimage and turn their hearts toward God can find inner freedom, moral clarity, and lasting peace.
outputs.L5:
Fle, Suffise, and For can be imagined as three simple ideas that work together in a creative way. **Fle** represents movement and curiosity—the desire to explore new places, thoughts, and possibilities. **Suffise** suggests having enough: enough patience, enough knowledge, or enough resources to continue forward. **For** points to purpose, reminding us that every action is stronger when it is done for a reason.

Together, these three words can form a small philosophy. We move like Fle, stay balanced through Suffise, and act with meaning through For. Whether in learning, work, or daily life, curiosity helps us begin, sufficiency helps us continue, and purpose helps us understand why the journey matters.

counterfactuals.output:
There is no single surviving “original” spelling for Chaucer’s poems, since they come down through manuscripts with variant spellings. Below is a standard Middle English text of Chaucer’s **“Balade de Bon Conseyl”** / **“Truth”**, retaining the traditional spelling rather than modernizing it.

## Balade de Bon Conseyl

Fle fro the pres, and dwelle with sothfastnesse,  
Suffyce unto thy good, though it be smal;  
For hord hath hate, and clymbyng tikelnesse,  
Pres hath envye, and wele blent overal.  
Savour no more than thee bihove shal;  
Reule wel thyself, that other folk canst rede;  
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

Tempest thee noght al croked to redresse,  
In trust of hir that turneth as a bal:  
Greet reste stant in litel besinesse.  
And eek be war to sporne ayeyns an al;  
Strive noght, as doth the crokke with the wal.  
Daunte thyself, that dauntest otheres dede;  
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

That thee is sent, receyve in buxomnesse,  
The wrastling for this world axeth a fal.  
Her nis non hoom, her nis but wildernesse:  
Forth, pilgrim, forth! Forth, beste, out of thy stal!  
Know thy contree, look up, thank God of al;  
Hold the hye wey, and lat thy gost thee lede:  
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.

Therfore, thou Vache, leve thyn old wrecchednesse;  
Unto the world leve now to be thral.  
Crye him mercy, that of his hy goodnesse  
Made thee of noght, and in especial  
Draw unto him, and pray in general  
For thee, and eek for other, hevenlich mede;  
And trouthe thee shal delivere, it is no drede.
